claims.text: An ultrathin aluminum-doped, alumina-forming coating improves the high-temperature oxidation resistance of zirconium-alloy nuclear-fuel cladding.
The coating forms a continuous and adherent Al2O3 barrier.
The Al2O3 barrier retards oxygen diffusion into the zirconium-alloy substrate.
Uncoated zirconium-alloy cladding develops a less-protective, rapidly growing oxide scale under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Physical vapor deposition can be used to apply the proposed aluminum-doped protective coating.
Rapid oxidation of zirconium-alloy cladding occurs in steam during transient accident conditions at approximately 1200–1500 °C.
Aluminum in the coating preferentially oxidizes at elevated temperature.
Preferential oxidation of aluminum produces a stable, protective Al2O3 layer.
Limiting oxygen ingress into the underlying zirconium alloy reduces rapid oxidation kinetics and associated degradation.
Coated cladding will have a significantly lower oxidation rate than uncoated cladding under identical high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Coated cladding will exhibit less weight gain than uncoated cladding.
Coated cladding will form less oxide scale than uncoated cladding.
The coated cladding will retain mechanical integrity suitable for service.
The oxidation-resistance improvement depends on the coating being defect-free, well-adhered, and thermally stable during transient exposure.
Effectiveness under prolonged exposure, cyclic thermal stress, and high-radiation conditions is undetermined.
The exact reduction in oxidation and long-term mechanical performance under reactor conditions are not established.
Weight gain per unit area and oxide-scale thickness can be used to compare oxidation behavior of coated and uncoated specimens.
Failure to achieve a statistically significant oxidation reduction, or occurrence of coating-induced mechanical degradation, would falsify the hypothesis.
